newsitem.title: UK: British parties bicker over voters' trust.
newsitem.headline: British parties bicker over voters' trust.

text.p: Britain's main political parties marked the fifth anniversary on Wednesday of the Conservatives' 1992 election win by scrapping over which of them voters could trust in the new election on May 1.

The Labour Party attacked the Conservatives for having broken 1992 manifesto pledges, while Labour came under sustained Conservative fire for executing an about-turn on a principle once dear to the party's hearts -- nationalisation.

The bitter exchanges broke out on a day when opinion polls said Labour's huge lead had begun to slip, though it still appeared firmly on course to oust Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives, in office since 1979.
Major said Labour leader Tony Blair had turned key areas of policy on their head to try to convince voters he would not raise taxes if he came to power.

"His manifesto is falling apart under the pressure of the general election. Saying one thing one day and another thing the next is no basis either for trust or for any belief in his competence," Major told a news conference.

In particular, he attacked Blair for considering privatising Britain's air traffic control services, a plan denounced by Labour transport spokesman Andrew Smith as irresponsible when the Conservatives first announced it.
"Open policy, open mouth, open mind, open warfare -- that is the real Labour Party," he said.
Conservative aides accompanying Major on a tour of Wales said he believed he had at last exposed Blair's "slipperiness" over policy.
Blair hit back, accusing Major of repeatedly failing to honour promises made to the electorate at the 1992 election, notably by raising taxes after pledging to cut them.

"Their record in government robs their manifesto of any shred of credibility. After five years of betrayal and broken promises, they no longer deserve the people's trust. They have become unfit to rule," Blair said.

An opinion poll in the Guardian newspaper opinion poll showed the lowest Labour lead of the campaign -- 12 points. A Daily Telegraph poll said the gap had narrowed to 19 points from 26 points on March 26.

The Guardian poll pointed to a huge Labour majority of 109 seats in the next parliament, but Conservative strategists believe the pressure of campaigning could cause the inexperienced Blair to falter at the final hurdle.

The Institute of Fiscal Studies added to the election debate with a report doubting whether either party would be able to keep taxes low, as they pledge, and maintain key elements of the welfare state such as the health service.

"Either the current shape of the welfare state will be maintained and the next government will have to spend - and tax - more than planned, or the welfare state will shrink and provide fewer services to fewer people," the report said.
Doubts over Labour tax plans caused voters to switch to the Conservatives at the last minute in 1992, giving the ruling party a fourth successive victory.
